title: The principal ideal problem

problem.name: The principal ideal problem
problem.statement_latex: Given a number field $K$ by a defining polynomial and an integral ideal $I\subseteq\mathcal O_K$ by a basis, determine whether $I=\alpha\mathcal O_K$; if so, output a compact representation of a generator $\alpha$. The relevant size parameters are the degree, logarithmic discriminant, ideal encoding length, and output precision. Complexity is measured in quantum gates and classical bit operations on the number-field and ideal encodings, with compact output.

quantum.headline_latex: Polynomial time in the input parameters, Hallgren and Biasse--Song principal-ideal algorithms.
quantum.headline_text: Polynomial time in the input parameters, Hallgren and Biasse–Song principal-ideal algorithms.
quantum.details_latex: Hallgren treats real quadratic fields. Biasse--Song give the arbitrary-degree result through their quantum $S$-unit algorithm, using compact generators and precision sufficient for the associated logarithmic lattice. The input parameters include degree, logarithmic discriminant and ideal encoding size. The principal-ideal theorem is the relevant search statement; the related class-group theorem has a GRH hypothesis.

classical.headline_latex: $L_{|\Delta_K|}[1/2,O(1)]$ under the standard index-calculus hypotheses in quadratic fields, relation-collection algorithms.
classical.headline_text: $L_{|\Delta_K|}[1/2,O(1)]$ under the standard index-calculus hypotheses in quadratic fields, relation-collection algorithms.
classical.details_latex: The classical work combines factor-base relations, unit computation and integer linear algebra. The quadratic-field family supplies the direct subexponential comparison for identical inputs and compact generators. In arbitrary degree, the strongest applicable classical bounds depend on the relationship between degree and discriminant; specialized field families also admit distinct relation-generation tradeoffs.

strength.description_latex: Subexponential to polynomial in the matched quadratic-field regime. Quantum Fourier methods supply the hidden-lattice information needed for the generator.

evidence.description_latex: Partial evidence for a classical separation, based on the established number-field algorithmic frontier. Polynomial quantum solvability follows from the cited theorems with their representation and precision assumptions.

hardware.description_latex: Polynomial logical space and coherent number-field arithmetic are required. Cryptographic-size computations belong to the fault-tolerant regime, with logical-qubit counts determined by field degree, coefficient precision and the chosen reversible arithmetic.
